about: Identifying features of prehistoric animals, written from museum, scientific and encyclopedia descriptions opened on 2026-10-06. Used to word each animal's prompt and to check each tile feature by feature. 'disagreement' is the researcher's full note; plan.json carries only the part that changes how the animal looks.

animals.name: Mosasaurus
features: Long, streamlined body with a deep, barrel-shaped chest; not thin or eel-like.
Large cone-shaped head, about one-seventh to one-eleventh of body length, ending in a short, blunt snout.
Big, stout, pointed teeth along both jaws; snout tip reaches only slightly past the front teeth.
Four paddle-shaped flippers: front pair broad and strong, hind pair smaller.
Long tail whose end bends downward and carries a two-lobed, shark-like fin; backbone runs into the lower lobe.
Skin of tiny overlapping scales that looks smooth from a distance; no crest, frill, spines or back fin.
Probably dark on the back and pale on the belly, like a great white shark.
Very large: about 11 to 12 metres, roughly seven adult people lying head to toe.
not_this: A frill, crest or row of spines along the back; this old error came from misidentified windpipe cartilage.
A thin, eel-like sea-serpent body with a straight pointed tail and no tail fin.
Film-style oversized animal with rough, armoured crocodile-like skin; real mosasaur scales were only a few millimetres across.
animals.tell_apart: Versus Tylosaurus: Mosasaurus has a short, blunt snout whose tip reaches only a little past the front teeth, a deeper barrel-shaped chest, robust jaws with big stout cutting teeth, and broad, strong front flippers. Tylosaurus has a proportionally longer, narrower snout ending in an obvious blunt, toothless bony knob that sticks out beyond the front teeth. If the snout tip shows a clear toothless knob, it is Tylosaurus, not Mosasaurus. Both share four flippers and a downturned two-lobed tail, so the head is the main clue.
animals.disagreement: Length is debated: older studies gave up to about 17 m for the largest species, while recent work (2014 to 2024) favours about 11 to 12 m. Mosasaurus is known mainly from skulls, so its tail fin and skin are inferred from related mosasaurs with preserved soft tissue (Prognathodon, Platecarpus); sources also differ on whether the scales were keeled or smooth, which is too fine to see in a whole-animal picture.

animals.name: Tylosaurus
features: Long, streamlined body with four paddle-shaped flippers.
Long, narrow cone-shaped head, about 13 to 14 percent of body length, with a longer snout than most mosasaurs.
Blunt, toothless bony knob at the snout tip, sticking out beyond the front teeth; lower jaw tip projects too.
Teeth all about the same size: pointed cones curving slightly backward.
Long tail with a clear downward bend near the end, carrying a two-lobed fin.
Tiny diamond-shaped scales in slanting rows, so the skin looks smooth from a distance; no back crest or fin.
Dark body colour, shown by fossil pigment, probably with a paler belly.
Large: about 9 to 13 metres depending on species, roughly five to eight adult people head to toe.
not_this: A fringe or crest running along the back, as in early paintings; it came from misidentified windpipe cartilage.
A long, snake-like neck and eel-thin body, as in 1870s drawings.
Teeth drawn right at the very tip of the snout, which hides the toothless knob.
animals.tell_apart: Versus Mosasaurus: the blunt, toothless bony knob projecting at the tip of the snout (with the lower jaw tip projecting too) is the giveaway, together with a proportionally longer, narrower snout and teeth of nearly equal size. Mosasaurus has a shorter, blunter snout with almost no projection past the teeth, a deeper barrel chest and broader front flippers. Body, flippers and tail are otherwise very alike, so the checker should look at the snout tip first.
animals.disagreement: Size figures differ: the Oceans of Kansas site (written by a Sternberg Museum curator) speaks of 15 m or more, while Wikipedia's recent figures give about 9.5 m at most for Tylosaurus proriger and 12 to 13 m for the largest species. The two-lobed tail fin is inferred from the bend in the tail bones and from related mosasaurs; no Tylosaurus tail fin has been found preserved.

animals.name: Kronosaurus
features: Huge, long head, over 2 metres: roughly a quarter of the animal's length, with a long, fairly narrow snout.
Very short, thick neck, so the head seems to join the body almost directly.
Massive, deep, heavy trunk.
Four large wing-like flippers; hind pair somewhat longer than the front pair.
Short tail, perhaps with a small fin; never long or whip-like.
Large cone-shaped teeth, biggest at the front of the jaws and smaller toward the back.
About 9 to 10.5 metres long: roughly five to six adult people head to toe.
not_this: The stretched body of the Harvard 'Plasterosaurus' mount: 12.8 m with extra vertebrae, about three metres too long.
A tall rounded dome or crest on the back of the skull, another invention of that plaster mount.
A long neck or a small head, which would make it the other kind of plesiosaur.
animals.tell_apart: Versus Plesiosaurus and Elasmosaurus: all three have four flippers, a stiff body and a short tail, but Kronosaurus has a giant head (over 2 m, about a quarter of its length) on a very short neck, with big cone-shaped teeth. Plesiosaurus and Elasmosaurus have tiny heads on very long necks with thin needle-like teeth. Kronosaurus is about 9 to 10.5 m, roughly three times the length of Plesiosaurus (about 3.5 m) and similar in total length to Elasmosaurus (about 10 m) but far bulkier. Its hind flippers are longer than its front ones, while in the two long-necked animals the front pair is the larger. Versus mosasaurs: Kronosaurus has four long wing-like flippers and a short tail with no large two-lobed fin.
animals.disagreement: Size: the Harvard mount is 12.8 m, but it was built with extra vertebrae and about one-third plaster; later studies and the Australian Museum give about 8 to 10.9 m. Skull length also varies by source and specimen (Australian Museum: at least 2.4 m; Wikipedia: 2.85 m for the Harvard skull but under 2 m for others). A 2021-22 proposal to rename the Harvard skeleton Eiectus longmani is disputed, and the tail is not known from joined-up fossils.

animals.name: Plesiosaurus
features: Small head, much narrower than long, with a bluntly triangular snout.
Long, slender neck, roughly as long as the body and tail put together.
Broad, stiff, turtle-like body, but with no shell.
Four long, narrow, pointed flippers; in adults the front pair is larger than the hind pair.
Short tail, far shorter than the neck.
Thin, needle-like teeth, slightly curved and pointing forward.
Neck held out fairly straight in front of the body, not reared up.
Small animal: about 3 to 3.5 metres, roughly twice the length of an adult person.
not_this: A swan-like neck lifted high out of the water.
A neck bent into snake-like coils; plesiosaur necks were rather stiff.
A neck far longer than the whole body (that is Elasmosaurus) or a big head (that is a pliosaur).
animals.tell_apart: Versus Elasmosaurus: Plesiosaurus is small (about 3 to 3.5 m, twice a person's length) and its neck is about as long as its body and tail together, so roughly half the animal, with about 40 neck bones. Elasmosaurus is about 10 m long and its neck (about 7 m, 72 neck bones) is roughly two-thirds of the animal, far longer than its body. In the picture, the neck of Plesiosaurus should look about equal to the rest of the animal, never double it. Versus Kronosaurus: Plesiosaurus has a tiny head on a long neck with needle teeth; Kronosaurus has a head over 2 m long on a very short neck with big cone teeth, and is about three times longer overall.
animals.disagreement: Scientists still debate how far plesiosaur necks could bend, though the sources agree that the swan pose and snake-like coils are wrong. Whether plesiosaurs had a small tail fin, and whether it stood upright or lay flat, is debated and not known for Plesiosaurus itself; skin was long thought smooth, but a 2025 fossil of another plesiosaur showed small scales on a flipper.

animals.name: Elasmosaurus
features: Extremely long neck, about 7 metres: roughly two-thirds of the whole animal and much longer than the body.
Very small, slender, triangular head at the end of the neck.
Long fang-like teeth at the front of the jaws, smaller ones behind, interlocking when shut.
Compact, streamlined, stiff body.
Four large paddle-shaped flippers, the front pair longer than the hind pair.
Short tail, tiny compared with the neck; a small tail fin is possible but unproven.
Neck held out roughly level in front of the body, with gentle curves at most.
About 10 metres long: roughly six adult people lying head to toe.
not_this: Neck raised high above the water like a swan; it could lift little more than its head out.
Neck coiled or looped like a snake, as in Charles Knight's old paintings.
Head placed on the short tail end (Cope's 1869 mistake), giving a short neck and a long tail.
animals.tell_apart: Versus Plesiosaurus: Elasmosaurus is about three times longer (about 10 m against 3 to 3.5 m) and its neck is far longer in proportion: about two-thirds of the animal, roughly twice the length of body and tail together, whereas the neck of Plesiosaurus only about equals its body and tail. The head looks even smaller against that neck. Versus Kronosaurus: similar total length, but Elasmosaurus is slender with a tiny head and an enormous neck, while Kronosaurus is bulky with a huge head and almost no neck.
animals.disagreement: Only one incomplete skeleton is known, and its limbs and shoulder and hip bones are missing, so the flippers are drawn from related elasmosaurs. Length figures differ: Wikipedia gives about 10.3 m with a 7.1 m neck, while older figures of 13 to 14 m (Cope's 13.7 m; 42 ft quoted in the 2013 PLOS ONE paper) still circulate. Studies also give a wide range for how far the neck could bend (about 75 to 177 degrees), but agree it could not hold a swan pose.

animals.name: Mixosaurus
features: Small fish-shaped reptile about 1 metre long: shorter than an adult person is tall.
Body deep at the front, narrowing to a slim tail region; longer-bodied than later ichthyosaurs.
Fairly large head with long, narrow jaws lined with small sharp teeth.
Four flippers; front pair clearly longer, hind pair less than two-thirds of their length.
An upright dorsal fin on the back, set well forward, above the rear edge of the front flippers.
Long tail with an upright fin whose upper lobe is a triangle, not a tall crescent moon.
Smooth skin with no scales.
not_this: A tall crescent, tuna-like tail and short compact body copied from Jurassic ichthyosaurs.
Dolphin features: flat horizontal tail flukes, a blowhole, or only two flippers.
An eel-like body with no back fin, as drawn before the 2020 soft-tissue fossils.
animals.tell_apart: Versus a dolphin: Mixosaurus has four flippers (a dolphin has two), an upright tail fin (a dolphin's tail flukes lie flat), a long thin snout full of small teeth, no blowhole, and it is only about 1 m long. Versus later ichthyosaurs such as Ichthyosaurus: those are compact and tuna-shaped with a tall crescent tail; Mixosaurus is longer-bodied with a long tail, a lower tail fin with a triangular upper lobe, a dorsal fin placed farther forward, and five-fingered flippers. Versus the earliest eel-shaped ichthyosaurs such as Cymbospondylus: Mixosaurus is shorter and deeper in front, with a clear dorsal fin and a relatively larger head.
animals.disagreement: Wikipedia describes a long tail with only a low fin, while the 2020 fossil study (Renesto and colleagues, Acta Palaeontologica Polonica) found a well-developed triangular upper tail lobe and a dorsal fin, so older finless, eel-like pictures are out of date. Size varies by source and species: most are 0.7 to 1 m, but the largest specimens exceed 2 m.

animals.name: Titanoboa
features: An enormous, heavy-bodied snake with no limbs, built like a giant boa or anaconda.
About 13 metres long (estimates run 12.8 to 14.3 m): seven to eight adult people head to toe.
Very thick body, about 1 metre across at its widest: hip to waist high on an adult.
Head small for the body, roughly 40 cm long, shaped like a boa's.
Many small, closely set teeth; no long fangs.
Shown in or beside water in a hot swampy forest, as an anaconda would be.
Colour and pattern are unknown: plain, natural boa or anaconda tones are acceptable, nothing bright or invented.
not_this: A cobra hood, a rattle or long venom fangs; it belonged to the boa group of constrictors.
Film-monster size far beyond about 14 metres.
Dinosaurs in the same scene; it lived about six million years after they died out.
animals.tell_apart: Closest living relatives: boas (subfamily Boinae). A 2013 conference abstract placed it nearest the boas of Madagascar and the Pacific islands, and the Florida Museum describes it as boa constrictor-like and related to boas and anacondas. Best living model: the green anaconda, for body proportions and a water-living habit. How it is reconstructed: about 186 fossils from some 30 individuals, mostly vertebrae and ribs, plus three broken skulls that are not yet formally described; scientists work out the link between vertebra size and body size in living snakes and apply it to the fossils. Length: about 12.8 m (plus or minus 2.2 m) from vertebra size compared with living boas, or about 14.3 m from a 40 cm skull using anaconda proportions; weight about 730 to 1,135 kg. Its exact appearance (colour, pattern, scale details) is unknown. Versus Vasuki indicus: the fossils give no reliable visible difference; the only fair cues are that Titanoboa is drawn as an anaconda-like boa in water (South America) and Vasuki as a python-like snake on land or marsh (India). Versus a living anaconda or python: the shape is the same, so only size separates them: more than twice the length of a large anaconda and about waist-thick, so the picture needs a scale cue such as a person or a tree trunk.
animals.disagreement: Length estimates differ: 12.8 m from vertebrae, about 14.3 m from the undescribed skulls, and museum pages quote anything from 42 to 50 feet. Body width (about 3 feet) and weight are scaled from living snakes, and none of the sources opened gives any fossil evidence for colour or pattern.

animals.name: Vasuki indicus
features: A very large, heavy-bodied snake with no limbs, drawn on the build of a big python.
Broad, round, cylinder-shaped body; not flattened from side to side like a swimming snake.
Length somewhere between 11 and 15 metres: about six to nine adult people head to toe.
Very thick body, in keeping with backbone pieces up to 11 cm wide; exact girth unknown.
Shown on land or marshy ground, resting or moving slowly; not swimming in open water.
Head is not known from fossils: a plain python-like head with no special features.
Colour and pattern unknown: plain, natural python-like tones are acceptable, nothing bright or invented.
not_this: A cobra hood, extra heads or other mythical features of the Hindu divine serpent Vasuki it is named after.
Long venom fangs or a rattle; it is thought to have killed by squeezing, like pythons and anacondas.
A sea-snake or eel shape with a flattened tail; the bones point to a round-bodied land or marsh snake.
animals.tell_apart: Closest relatives: Vasuki belongs to Madtsoiidae, an extinct snake family with no living members; its nearest relatives are other extinct madtsoiids (Madtsoia pisdurensis and Gigantophis). Best living model: large pythons (Python and the reticulated python), because the vertebrae look broadly similar and big pythons live in similar swampy habitats; its ambush hunting by squeezing is compared to anacondas and big pythons. How it is reconstructed: from only 27 backbone pieces of one fully grown animal found in the Panandhro lignite mine in Kutch, Gujarat; no skull was found. Sideways-pointing rib attachments on the vertebrae suggest a broad, cylindrical body. Length: 10.9 to 12.2 m by one formula (vertebra width scaled against living boas) or 14.5 to 15.2 m by another (vertebra width scaled against many kinds of living snakes); the authors say both should be treated with caution because the rear of the backbone is missing. The head, tail, skin, colour, pattern and exact thickness are all unknown, so almost everything in a picture beyond 'giant thick snake' is informed guesswork. Versus Titanoboa: no reliable visible difference can be drawn from the fossils; Titanoboa had slightly larger vertebrae and is modelled on an anaconda in water, while Vasuki is modelled on a python on land or marsh. Versus a living python or anaconda: only size differs, far longer than the longest living snake (the reticulated python), so the picture needs a scale cue such as a person or a tree.
animals.disagreement: The two length formulas disagree (about 11 to 12 m against 14.5 to 15 m), so it is unresolved whether Vasuki was longer than Titanoboa; its vertebrae are slightly smaller. The authors favour a land or marsh lifestyle but say a water-living one cannot be completely ruled out.
